title: 17-Year-Old Sienna Toohey Shatters Leisel Jones' Age Record
summary: To kick off the second night of Australian Swimming Trials, 17-year-old Sienna Toohey put together a statement swim. The Albury native threw down a 1:05.97 100 breaststroke to break an iconic age record and become the fastest Australian in the post-supersuit era. The 17-year-old age record previously belonged to all-time great Leisel Jones. She posted a 1:06.37 at the same age at the 2003 World Championships in Barcelona, which was a new world record at the time. Toohey had previously been nipping at that record's heels when she went her previous lifetime best of 1:06.43 at Australia's Age Championships in April. Tonight, Toohey distinguished herself from her old best and 17-year-old Jones with a blistering first 50 of 30.58. This made her too quick to catch on the second 50. She now moves into third all time among Aussies, and she surpasses Chelsea Hodges as the fastest post-supersuit swimmer from the nation. The swim also proves hopeful for Australia on the contemporary world stage. This season, she checks in as the 5th fastest performer. Among both Commonwealth and Pan Pac countries, which she has punched tickets for, she sits among the top three. A 1:05.97 100 breast would've qualified for the Paris 2024 and Singapore 2025 finals. Australia has not had an Olympic or Worlds qualifier in the event since 2019. On the women's medley relay front, if Toohey can replicate this speed, it places Australia as an even clearer world #2 behind the United States. At the 2025 World Championships, the Aussies earned the silver, about three seconds behind the Americans and two seconds ahead of China with Ella Ramsay on breaststroke. Ramsay also had a big swim of 1:06.70 for runner-up tonight, which is a new best for the 21-year-old. Sienna Toohey is definitely a name to watch.
why_it_matters: Toohey's achievement shows that hard work and talent can rewrite records even at a young age, and it highlights how advances in training and fair equipment rules create space for new stars to emerge in competitive sports.

background_read: Leisel Jones is one of Australia's most decorated swimmers, having won nine Olympic medals (including three golds) and setting multiple world records in breaststroke.

The 'supersuit era' (2008–2009) saw dozens of world records fall due to full-body polyurethane suits; FINA banned them in 2010, so times set since are labeled 'post-supersuit' to indicate a more even playing field.
Sienna Toohey hails from Albury, a regional city on the New South Wales–Victoria border, showing that elite talent can emerge outside major metropolitan centers.
The Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacific Championships are two major international meets where Australia regularly competes against top swimming nations like the USA, Canada, and China.

perspectives.description: Fans celebrate Toohey's breakout swim as a sign that Australian women's breaststroke is regaining strength. Her time could bring medals in upcoming international meets.
Some worry about the pressure placed on a teenager to keep delivering top performances, and note that comparing eras is tricky even after the supersuit ban due to other technological changes.
Historical comparisons are a useful way to measure progress, but swimming times are also influenced by pool technology, nutrition, and training science.
If Toohey maintains this trajectory, she could become a medal contender at the 2028 Olympics and spark new investment in youth swimming programs in regional Australia.
